content: Lactuca virosa, commonly referred to as Wild Lettuce, Bitter Lettuce, Opium Lettuce, or Poisonous Lettuce, is a plant related to common lettuce (Lactuca sativa). It is legally classified as an ethnobotanical in the United States, meaning it can be grown, purchased, and owned without the need for a prescription or license, as it is not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Historically, Lactuca virosa was utilized by physicians in the 19th century as an alternative when opium was unavailable. In 1911, the Council of the Pharmaceutical Society of Great Britain conducted extensive research on the plant and identified two key active compounds responsible for its effects: lactucopicrin and lactucin. The plant gained renewed interest in the United States during the 1970s. The effects of Lactuca virosa are often compared to those of opium, although the plant does not contain any opiates. Its effects are typically felt quickly but are short-lived, lasting anywhere from 30 minutes to a few hours, and gradually taper off. The plant has been used for its sedative and analgesic properties, serving as an anesthetic and a sleep aid. It has also been used recreationally. Extracts and oils derived from the plant are commonly added to teas to promote sleep. Additionally, the leaves, though more bitter than typical salad greens, are sometimes included in salads. Lactuca virosa can also be consumed in other forms. The dried leaves or a sticky resinous extract from the leaves can be smoked. Beverages can be prepared by soaking the leaves in alcohol. The plant contains flavonoids, which exhibit potent antioxidant properties, as well as coumarins and N-methyl-β-phenethylamine. Furthermore, Lactuca virosa has been identified as a galactagogue, meaning it can enhance breast milk production in lactating women, particularly when used in combination with alfalfa.
